candidates.current_role: Texas state senator, District 11, since 2023; president of Middleton Oil Company
candidates.background: Mayes Middleton is a Galveston-area oil and gas executive, rancher and attorney who earned his law degree from the University of Texas School of Law in 2008. He served two terms in the Texas House, where he chaired the House Freedom Caucus, before winning a state Senate seat in 2022. He won the Republican nomination for attorney general by defeating U.S. Rep. Chip Roy in the May 26, 2026 runoff with about 56 percent of the vote.

priorities.text: Campaigns on backing President Trump's border security agenda and deportation orders, including suing cities that he says violate the state ban on sanctuary policies.
Campaigns on election integrity, including enforcement of Texas voter ID laws so that only qualified U.S. citizens vote.
Campaigns on zero tolerance for violent crime and on reining in district attorneys he says refuse to enforce state law.
Campaigns on keeping transgender women out of women's restrooms, locker rooms and sports.
Campaigns on open records enforcement and a "DOGE Texas" approach to waste and fraud in government spending.
Says he will protect oil and gas jobs and Texas energy independence.

promises.text: Says he will create a standalone election integrity division in the attorney general's office with law enforcement powers.
Says he will sue local officials who obstruct federal immigration enforcement and seek civil and criminal penalties and removal from office.
Says he will seek stronger bonds for dangerous offenders and increased consequences for district attorneys who do not enforce state law.
Says he will sue corporations for deceptive trade practices and oppose foreign adversaries buying Texas assets.

record.text: Authored Senate Bill 8 (2025), which requires people in public schools, universities and government buildings to use restrooms matching their sex at birth; Gov. Abbott signed it in September 2025.
Sponsored and passed the Save Women's Sports Act, which bars transgender women from competing in women's collegiate sports.
Sponsored a 2025 bill allowing schools to set aside class time for prayer and Bible reading.
Passed legislation allowing the attorney general's office to take election fraud cases without waiting for a local prosecutor, according to a candidate profile.
Voted with the Senate majority for Senate Bill 2 (2025), which created the state's education savings account program; all Senate Democrats and one Republican opposed it.
Voted to acquit Attorney General Ken Paxton at his 2023 impeachment trial; the Tribune reported he had been among senators considering a vote to convict.
In 2025 sponsored a bill to limit offshore wind projects, and in 2022 wrote to the Biden administration opposing a proposed wind farm off the Galveston coast.
Cosponsored a bill by Sen. Nathan Johnson strengthening consumer protections for commercial genetic testing.

notes.text: Put more than $16 million of his own money into the primary and runoff, according to the Tribune in May 2026; later Tribune reporting put his self-funding above $20 million.

Over about 15 years he donated millions to conservative candidates and groups, including most initial members of the House Freedom Caucus, and was the main funder of Matt Krause's 2022 primary challenge to Ken Paxton. Chip Roy accused him of buying endorsements; Middleton did not respond to that request for comment.
Ran ads calling himself "MAGA Mayes" and told NBC DFW, "I am 100% pro-Trump." Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick endorsed him in the runoff.
Critics, including his runoff opponent, noted he has practiced law only for his family company and has little courtroom experience.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Supports displaying the Ten Commandments in public school classrooms and has said "there is no such thing as separation of church and state."

q_abortion.summary: Pledges to uphold Texas pro-life laws and has donated to Texas Right to Life.

q_deportation.summary: Has said "We have to deport all illegal immigrants. Not some. All," and calls backing federal deportation efforts his top priority.

q_gun_laws.summary: Lists co-authoring the 2021 permitless carry law among his accomplishments; he has not been found addressing background checks or red flag laws directly.

q_bail.summary: Says he opposes quick low-bond releases of dangerous offenders and will push for stronger bonds.

q_election_fraud.summary: Proposes a standalone election integrity unit with law enforcement powers and stronger enforcement of voter ID laws.

q_trans_minors.summary: Pledges to stop efforts to "confuse our children with gender ideology" and authored laws restricting transgender access to sports and restrooms; no statement specific to medical treatment for minors was found.

q_foreign_land.summary: Pledges to oppose foreign adversaries buying Texas assets.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted for Senate Bill 2 in 2025, which created the education savings account program.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Says he will protect oil and gas jobs and sponsored a 2025 bill to limit offshore wind projects.

issue_notes.summary: Has called the U.S. Supreme Court decision in Plyler v. Doe, which guarantees public schooling to undocumented children, "terrible" and supports overturning it.
Attacked Nathan Johnson in the general election, saying Johnson would "fight to get men in your little girl's restroom and locker room."
Says he rejected the state pension and health plan and donates his state salary to charity, and pledges to hold officials accountable for profiting from office.

candidates.current_role: Texas state senator, District 16 (Dallas), since 2019; attorney at Thompson Coburn
candidates.background: Nathan Johnson is a Dallas business litigator and mediator with a physics degree from the University of Arizona and a law degree from the University of Texas at Austin. He won his North Dallas Senate seat in 2018 by defeating Republican incumbent Don Huffines, and says he has passed 134 bills since 2019. He earlier composed music for the Dragon Ball Z animated series. He won the Democratic nomination in the May 26, 2026 runoff over former Galveston Mayor Joe Jaworski.

priorities.text: Campaigns on returning the attorney general's office to core duties such as child support collection, legal opinions, public finance review and open government.
Campaigns on enforcing consumer protection and antitrust laws against price gouging, junk fees, scams and unfair competition.
Campaigns on investigating and prosecuting public corruption "irrespective of political party."
Campaigns on an office independent of both political parties and of any presidential administration.
Campaigns on public safety through partnership with district attorneys and the office's own authority over identity theft, cybercrime, Medicaid fraud and some human trafficking cases.

promises.text: Says he will make improving the child support division a priority, citing complaints about delays and service.
Says he will join other states in suing the Trump administration over actions he considers illegal, while saying he will not sue "for fun."
Says he will produce recommendations to the Legislature on how consumer protection, competition and employment laws apply to artificial intelligence within his first 30 days.
Says he will not defend the Ten Commandments classroom display law while appeals continue and will not devote resources to enforcing Senate Bill 8, the 2025 restroom law.
Says he will audit Deloitte and other state vendors after the Department of Public Safety failed to transmit more than 150,000 voter registration applications.
Says he will review actions taken under Ken Paxton and support House Democrats' litigation against the 2025 mid-decade redistricting plan.

record.text: Voted to convict Ken Paxton at his 2023 impeachment trial, as part of the Senate minority.
Voted against Senate Bill 2 in 2025, which created the education savings account program; all Senate Democrats opposed it.
Filed bills as a senator to restore abortion access and to expand Medicaid.
Authored a bill strengthening consumer protections for commercial genetic testing, which Mayes Middleton cosponsored.
Voted for Senate Bill 2972 (2025), a campus protest law, which he noted drew bipartisan support.

Says his legislative work secured $2 billion for backup power at water plants, nursing homes and first responder facilities, and updated state law on data privacy, artificial intelligence and cybersecurity.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Texas AFL-CIO, Sierra Club, Everytown for Gun Safety and the Texas Federation of Teachers, according to his campaign site.
Had about $1 million in his campaign account in late September 2026, roughly half of Middleton's total.
Former Republican state Sen. John Carona, a past supporter of the Texas Tribune, is one of his larger donors, according to the Tribune's disclosure.

q_ten_commandments.summary: Called a 5th Circuit ruling allowing classroom Ten Commandments displays unconstitutional and said he would not defend the law while appeals continue.

q_abortion.summary: Filed bills in the Senate to restore abortion access.

q_gun_laws.summary: Is endorsed by Everytown for Gun Safety, a gun safety advocacy group; no direct statement on specific gun laws was found.

q_deportation.summary: Says the office should assist federal immigration enforcement "as appropriate" and block federal actions that "go too far," and rejects "shock and awe" tactics he says violate the Constitution.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against Senate Bill 2 (2025), which created education savings accounts.

q_medicaid.summary: Filed bills in the Senate to expand Medicaid.

issue_notes.summary: Released a plan in August 2026 to use the office to review how existing laws apply to harms from artificial intelligence, including AI-driven scams and data privacy.
Called for an audit of state broadband funding over concerns that a company tied to Elon Musk received a favorable deal.
Says the state should secure the border against drug smuggling, human trafficking and cross-border crime without surrendering state sovereignty.

candidates.current_role: Texas Comptroller of Public Accounts (appointed) since August 1, 2026
candidates.background: Don Huffines is a Dallas real estate developer who co-founded Huffines Communities and holds a business degree from the University of Texas at Austin. He served one term in the Texas Senate (District 16, 2015 to 2019), lost reelection to Nathan Johnson in 2018, and challenged Gov. Greg Abbott in the 2022 Republican primary. He won the 2026 Republican comptroller primary with about 57 percent over acting Comptroller Kelly Hancock and others, and Abbott appointed him comptroller for the rest of 2026.

priorities.text: Campaigns on auditing government spending, which he calls "DOGE-ing Texas," and returning savings to taxpayers as property tax relief.
Campaigns on reducing and ultimately eliminating property taxes, saying Texans should not spend their lives "paying perpetual rent through property taxes."
Campaigns on implementing and promoting the state's education savings account program.
Campaigns on reducing regulations he says raise housing and business costs, and on favoring Texas-based companies in state contracting.
Campaigns on studying the cost of illegal immigration to the state and ensuring public money does not benefit undocumented immigrants.

promises.text: Pledged not to take a state salary, and declined it as his first official act.
Says he will audit state spending and highway construction contracts.
Says he will prioritize marketing the $1 billion education savings account program so parents know it exists.
Says he will work with state leaders on property tax relief in the next legislative session.

record.text: Ordered a performance review of the comptroller's office in August 2026, citing a directive from state leaders to cut agency spending by 3 percent.
In August 2026 urged cities and counties to lower property tax rates because of rising sales tax collections, and announced performance reviews of school district spending.
As a state senator, led the effort to abolish the Dallas County Schools bus agency after uncovering financial problems that led to a federal bribery investigation.
Authored a property tax exemption for surviving spouses of first responders killed in the line of duty.
Filed a bill as a senator to study the cost of a private school voucher program; it did not pass.

notes.text: Gov. Abbott appointed him comptroller on July 2, 2026, after acting Comptroller Kelly Hancock resigned; Sarah Eckhardt called the appointment a way to install a loyalist before voters decide.
Largely self-funded his primary campaign and reported $11.7 million cash on hand in January 2026; endorsed by U.S. Sen. Ted Cruz.
Founded the Huffines Liberty Foundation after leaving the Senate.

q_prop_tax_eliminate.summary: Has campaigned on eliminating property taxes, and his foundation proposed phasing school maintenance and operations taxes to zero using state surplus.

q_spending_cap.summary: His foundation proposed capping state spending growth at 3 percent, a different formula than population plus inflation.

q_vouchers.summary: Supports taxpayer-funded private school stipends and says competition will improve public schools.

q_abortion.summary: Backs banning abortion in all cases, according to the Tribune.

issue_notes.summary: Has proposed repealing the state franchise tax, which the comptroller's office administers.
Says "Local governments must be more conservative in how they spend, period."

candidates.background: Sarah Eckhardt is an attorney with a law degree and a master's in public affairs from the University of Texas at Austin. She was an assistant Travis County attorney, a Travis County commissioner (elected 2006) and Travis County judge (2015 to 2020) before winning a 2020 special election to the Texas Senate. She won the 2026 Democratic comptroller primary with about 64 percent, and she keeps her Senate seat if she loses.

priorities.text: Campaigns on making the comptroller a "watchdog" over state spending rather than "a lapdog for the rich and powerful."
Campaigns on auditing the state's education savings account program, which she calls the "voucher scheme."
Campaigns on stopping no-bid contracts to large donors and scrutinizing corporate tax incentives, including state incentives for AI data centers.
Campaigns on protecting public schools and reporting the costs of state underinvestment in education, health care and other services.
Campaigns on breaking what she calls 30 years of one-party rule.

promises.text: Says she will "audit the daylights" out of the school voucher program, including who receives the money and how it is spent.
Says that on day one she will review all no-bid contracts made under the governor's emergency orders.
Says she will restore rigorous performance evaluations of state agencies.
Says she will expose the cost to Texans of the state's decision not to expand Medicaid.

record.text: Voted against Senate Bill 2 in 2025, which created the education savings account program; all Senate Democrats opposed it.
Authored an Academic Fresh Start bill that Gov. Abbott vetoed in 2023; she refiled it in 2025 and Abbott signed it.
Passed a 2025 law exempting paramedics from tuition and fees at public colleges and universities.
As Travis County judge, issued a March 2020 COVID-19 disaster declaration that canceled South by Southwest and a stay-at-home order.
As Travis County judge, oversaw creation of the county's first public defender's office in 2019.

notes.text: In 2020 the State Commission on Judicial Conduct sanctioned her over a 2017 protest hat and a 2019 joke about Gov. Abbott; a special court of review overturned the sanction in 2022.
Briefly ran for the 10th Congressional District in late 2025 before switching to the comptroller race on the final filing day.
In September 2023 placed a statement in the Senate Journal criticizing Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick's conduct during the Paxton impeachment trial and declined to retract it.

q_vouchers.summary: Voted against creating the education savings account program in 2025 and calls it a "voucher scheme" she would audit.

q_school_funding.summary: Campaigns on protecting public schools and says underinvestment in public education has harmed Texans.

q_medicaid.summary: Says the comptroller should expose the cost of the state's refusal to expand Medicaid.

issue_notes.summary: Says the Texas Enterprise Fund has shifted from manufacturing jobs toward investment firms and that clawbacks have declined.
Her platform highlights securing senior property tax exemptions.

candidates.background: Dawn Buckingham is an oculoplastic surgeon with a bachelor's degree from the University of Texas at Austin and a medical degree from the University of Texas Medical Branch. She served on the Lake Travis ISD board and represented Senate District 24 from 2017 to 2023. She became the first woman to lead the General Land Office in 2023 and was unopposed in the 2026 Republican primary.

priorities.text: Campaigns on border security, which she calls a pillar of her campaign, including use of state land for border barriers and immigration enforcement.
Campaigns on protecting the oil and gas industry, which she links to national security, and on developing geothermal, nuclear and natural gas power on state lands.
Campaigns on growing Permanent School Fund contributions to public education.
Campaigns on serving veterans through the Veterans Land Board, veterans homes and cemeteries.
Campaigns on disaster recovery and flood mitigation funding.
Campaigns on restoring the Alamo and protecting Texas history from what she calls "revision."

promises.text: Says she will complete a new Alamo visitor center and museum.
Says the Alamo Cenotaph "will never be moved."
Says she will protect 2.5 million oil and gas jobs.

record.text: Launched the Jocelyn Initiative to commit General Land Office resources to detaining and deporting people in the country illegally, and in November 2024 pledged state land to support federal deportation efforts.
Declared Rio Grande islands Texas territory to give the Department of Public Safety operational control, and bought riverfront property for a border wall right-of-way, according to her campaign.
Ordered federal contractors to stop clearing a state border tract near Big Bend after a lawsuit from Presidio leaders.
Says her office has delivered over $9 billion in disaster recovery, $1 billion in flood mitigation and nearly $6 billion for public education; these are campaign figures.
Sued the Biden administration over endangered species listings and efforts to halt liquefied natural gas exports, according to her campaign.
As a state senator, filed a bill to impose civil penalties on faithless presidential electors.

notes.text: Former Alamo Trust CEO Kate Rogers left in October 2025 after Buckingham criticized an Indigenous Peoples' Day post as "woke"; Rogers sued Buckingham and others, and in August 2026 a federal judge allowed most claims, including a First Amendment claim against Buckingham, to proceed.
Endorsed by President Trump, House Speaker Dustin Burrows, the National Border Patrol Council and the Texas Oil and Gas Association; reported about $3.2 million cash on hand on June 30, 2026.
In 2023 she relayed a Texas A&M professor's lecture remarks criticizing Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick; the professor was investigated and cleared about two weeks later.

candidates.current_role: Investor; former chair of the Tarrant County Republican Party
candidates.background: Bo French grew up in Midland in an oil family, worked as an energy trader for about a decade starting in 1994, and later owned security businesses in the Middle East and worked in private equity. He chaired the Tarrant County Republican Party from 2023 until resigning to run statewide in 2025. He narrowly defeated incumbent Railroad Commissioner Jim Wright in the May 2026 Republican runoff.

priorities.text: Campaigns on protecting the oil and gas industry, which he calls "the most important industry on the planet."
Campaigns on ending diversity, equity and inclusion programs, funding and contracting practices at the commission.
Campaigns on reducing what he calls "overbearing regulation" of oil and gas operators.
Campaigns on ending Chinese government influence in the Texas oil industry and stopping what he calls an "Islamic invasion" of Texas.
Campaigns on a "pro-family credentialing program" for operators and on promoting U.S.-Israel partnerships.

promises.text: Says his first legislative priority as commissioner will be expanding Senate Bill 17, the 2025 foreign land ownership law, to include Muslim-majority countries.
Says he will enforce the state ban on land ownership by hostile foreign interests.

notes.text: Endorsed after the runoff by Gov. Abbott, Lt. Gov. Patrick, Railroad Commissioners Wayne Christian and Christi Craddick, and the Texas Oil and Gas Association PAC.
Major donors include a PAC backed by Tim Dunn and Farris Wilks, which gave $773,500 by June 30, 2026.

In 2024 fellow Republicans condemned his repeated use of slurs against political opponents in social media posts, and he drew calls to resign as county chair after a poll asking whether Jews or Muslims were a bigger threat to America.
At CPAC in 2026 he said Texas should ban Islam and called for deporting 100 million people; he has also said Texas should not recognize children born to undocumented parents as citizens.

A September 2026 post calling UT student fans "foreigners" who displaced Americans drew criticism from several Republicans; Karl Rove and U.S. Sen. John Cornyn said they would not vote for him. French stood by the remark.
Has not confirmed participation in an October 22 debate that Jon Rosenthal announced.

candidates.background: Jon Rosenthal is an oil field mechanical engineer with more than 20 years in and around the oil and gas industry as an engineer, project manager and team leader. He has represented House District 135, around Cypress, since 2019 and is serving his fourth term. He was unopposed in the 2026 Democratic primary and did not seek reelection to the House.

priorities.text: Campaigns on enforcing existing commission rules and barring new permits for companies that violate them.
Campaigns on ending routine flaring and venting of natural gas except in emergencies, with leak detection requirements and help for small operators.
Campaigns on fair, predictable gas utility rates, opposing junk fees and charges for preventable storm failures.
Campaigns on a more accessible commission with regional liaisons, evening hearings and language access.
Calls himself a "drill, baby, drill" Democrat who supports an "all of the above" energy strategy.

promises.text: Says he will require gas capture with enforceable timelines, supported by compliance clinics for small operators.
Says he will expand well plugging, seek more industry funding for it and publish public dashboards.
Says he will apply stricter prudence reviews before utilities recover extraordinary costs and require plain-language bills.
Says he will set up a 24/7 complaint hotline with case tracking and neighborhood air monitoring pilots.
Says he will strengthen enforcement of natural gas weatherization requirements.
Says data centers should file water and power resource plans before construction and should not be built next to homes.

record.text: Has served in the Texas House since 2019, representing a northwest Houston district.

notes.text: Endorsed by the Sierra Club, Texas AFL-CIO, the Houston Chronicle and Austin American-Statesman editorial boards, and former GOP Railroad Commission candidate Hawk Dunlap; Republican strategist Karl Rove said he would vote for him.
Outraised French in the third quarter of 2026, with about $488,000; neither candidate received money from major oil and gas industry PACs in that period.
French's campaign linked Rosenthal to the Bolshevik Revolution, a claim the Forward criticized as antisemitic.

q_fossil_priority.summary: Backs an "all of the above" energy strategy, supports oil and gas production and geothermal, and has said federal clean energy laws helped meet energy needs.

q_ethics.summary: Says he wants to reduce the influence of industry money and lobbyists on the commission.

issue_notes.summary: Supports statewide rules for data centers combined with a local right to disallow construction.

attorney-general.text: The attorney general is the state's lawyer: defends state laws and agencies in court, issues legal opinions, collects child support, enforces consumer protection and antitrust law, and has limited direct criminal authority (for example, Medicaid fraud, cybercrime and some election cases). Local district attorneys handle most criminal prosecutions.

comptroller.text: The comptroller is the state's chief financial officer: collects state taxes, issues the revenue estimate that limits the Legislature's budget, manages hundreds of state contracts, and administers the $1 billion education savings account program created in 2025.

land-commissioner.text: The land commissioner runs the General Land Office: manages about 13 million acres of state land and mineral leases, oversees part of the Permanent School Fund, administers federal disaster recovery aid, chairs the Veterans Land Board, manages the Alamo, and sits on the Legislative Redistricting Board.

agriculture-commissioner.text: The agriculture commissioner runs the Texas Department of Agriculture (about 755 staff): licensing and fees for agricultural industries including hemp, school nutrition programs, pest and animal health response, and marketing programs such as Go Texan. Fuel pump inspection moved to another agency in 2019.

railroad-commissioner.text: The three-member Railroad Commission does not regulate railroads. It regulates oil and gas production, pipelines, natural gas utilities and their weather readiness, coal and uranium surface mining, hydrogen storage and carbon dioxide storage. Commissioners serve six-year terms.
